messages.author: afb5e9b80b8608ec
messages.subject: spMsPGOcc - difficulty with convergence
parts:
Hi all,

I'm having some trouble getting the spatial covariates of a spMsPGOcc model to converge, and was hoping for some guidance.

I'm fitting the model below with data from 53 sites and 28 species. Currently the community-level means and variances all appear to converge, and at the species-level all occurrence, detection, and phi spatial covariance variables appear to converge, but there are always 3-4 species for which sigma.sq does not converge (rhat >1.1).

Do I just need to increase the number of samples? I know the vignette says these are some of the most computationally intensive models and may take hours or days to run (this model took ~8 hours). I also thought about changing the initial sigma.sq values - would this help? Is there something else I haven't considered?

 Any guidance would be appreciated! 

msom.occ.null1.spatial6 <- spMsPGOcc(occ.formula = ~ scale(dist_to_edge) + scale(dist_to_roads) + scale(X500_FC_PER),
                                     det.formula = ~1,
                                     data = data.msom,
                                     n.batch = 60000, # *25 = 1,500,000 samples
                                     batch.length = 25, 
                                     accept.rate = 0.43, 
                                     cov.model = "exponential",  
                                     n.omp.threads = 1, 
                                     verbose = TRUE,
                                     NNGP = TRUE,
                                     n.neighbors = 5,
                                     n.report = 10000,
                                     n.burn = 500000,
                                     n.thin = 50,
                                     n.chains = 3,
)

Best wishes,
Tasha

(P.S. Thanks to Jeff for developing this package :) )

messages.author: 0b274a0ee3490d75
messages.subject: Re: spMsPGOcc - difficulty with convergence
parts:
Hi Tasha,

spMsPGOcc models can be quite difficult to work with, particularly for communities larger than 5-10 species or so, and when some of your species are quite rare. In general, I now recommend using the "spatial factor multispecies occupancy" (sfMsPGOcc) model approach as opposed to spMsPGOcc given that it: (1) is substantially faster; (2) performs equally as well or better than spMsPGOcc in a variety of situations as shown in the paper I link to in the next sentence; (3) and often will be easier to get to converge than spMsPGOcc unless you have ideal circumstances (e.g., only a few species and not super rare). So, I might suggest trying sfMsPGocc instead, which is described in depth in this vignette and this paper. Here are a couple other things to think about as well. 
  • 53 sites is a relatively small number of sites to use for a complex spatial occupancy model, so fitting any sort of spatial model will likely be difficult. Because there are not all that many spatial locations, there is limited information that is available to the model to try and estimate the spatial parameters, which is likely why convergence is leading to difficulties. The spMsPGocc function estimates a separate spatial random effect for each species, which is very difficult to do, even when there are a substantially larger number of spatial locations (e.g., hundreds). This is further reason to try out the sfMsPGOcc function, as it will likely be easier to estimate than spMsPGOcc.
  • I see are not including any covariates on detection probability. If there is unmodeled heterogeneity in detection probability, this could also contribute to spatial models being difficult to converge, so that could be something else to think about if you continue to not get the models to work.
  • It may also be helpful to ensure that non-spatial models (e.g., msPGOcc) can converge successfully before going to far down a rabbit hole with convergence issues in the spatial model. Sometimes you may just have too many rare species that you are trying to model.
  • Setting initial values is always useful, particularly for the spatial parameters. Whether you continue with spMsPGOcc or go to sfMsPGOcc, setting initial values based on the values of a preliminary run can often help with convergence difficulties. This vignette talks about some convergence problems with different types of spatial occupancy models.
 Hope that helps!

Jeff

messages.author: afb5e9b80b8608ec
messages.subject: Re: spMsPGOcc - difficulty with convergence
parts:
Dear Jeff,

I have followed your advice and tried the sfMsPGocc, following this vignette, which successfully converged. 

If you don't mind it would be great if you could sense-check the outcome for me. The sfMsPGocc had a lower WAIC value than the msPGOcc, and indicated a better model fit for a couple of species in the community (Bayesian p-values). However when examining the posterior summaries of the spatial factor loadings, all 95% credible intervals contain zero: 


From this I have interpreted that the spatial factor is not an important driver of species-specific occurrence across space, and it would be better to continue with the msPGOcc  (cross-validation also suggests the msPGOcc performs better).

Would you agree with this interpretation?

Best wishes,
Tasha

messages.author: 0b274a0ee3490d75
messages.subject: Re: spMsPGOcc - difficulty with convergence
parts:
Hi Tasha,

Glad to hear you were able to get the model to converge. The large uncertainty is likely related to the fairly small number of spatial locations used to fit the spatial model. Spatial occupancy models can be data hungry, particularly when it comes to having a large number of sites, so fitting a model with 53 sites may show substantial uncertainty in the model parameters as a result and will often perform worse with cross-validation (since that requires fitting models with an even smaller number of spatial locations). I think it is reasonable to conclude that you can continue with msPGOcc given the small number of sites and hence difficulty to estimate a spatial process, the cross-validation results, and large uncertainty in the factor loadings.

Kind regards,

Jeff

Hi Jeff,

That's great thank you for the advice!

I have another question if you don't mind. I tried to adapt the code shared in this thread: Plot of predicted covariate effect on occupancy probability with stPGOcc object? and think I might have missed something when trying to apply it to a multi-species rather than a single-species model due to not being clear on the output's structure. I am aiming to create a plot predicting the effect of the model covariates (here distance to forest edge) on community occupancy probability. I have included the code below, could you please let me know if I've missed the mark?

Best wishes,
Tasha

# Create a set of values across the range of observed forest edge values
edge.pred.vals <- seq(min(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge),
                       max(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge),
                       length.out = 500)

# Scale predicted values by mean and standard deviation used to fit the model
edge.pred.vals.scale <- (edge.pred.vals - mean(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge)) /
  sd(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge)

# Predict occupancy across forest edge values at mean values of all other variable
pred.df_mine <- as.matrix(data.frame(intercept = 1, dist_to_edge = edge.pred.vals.scale,
                                     dist_to_roads = 0, X500_FC_PER = 0))

#excluded following lines 
#X.0_mine <- array(pred.df_mine, dim = c(nrow(pred.df_mine), 1, ncol(pred.df_mine)))
#dimnames(X.0_mine)[[3]] <- c('(Intercept)', 'scale(dist_to_edge)',

#X.0_mine<-as.matrix(X.0_mine)

out.pred_mine <- predict(msom.occ.null1_read, pred.df_mine)
psi.0.quants <- apply(out.pred_mine$psi.0.samples, c(3), quantile, #here is where I think I may have overlooked something
                      prob = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
psi.plot.dat <- data.frame(psi.med = psi.0.quants[2, ],
                           psi.low = psi.0.quants[1, ],

                           dist_to_edge = edge.pred.vals.scale)

#back-transforming for plotting
psi.plot.dat$dte_bt<-(psi.plot.dat$dist_to_edge*sd(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge)) + mean(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge)

  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = psi.low, ymax = psi.high), fill = 'grey70') +
  geom_line() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = 'Distance to forest edge (m)', y = 'Occupancy \n Probability')

Hi Tasha,

spMsPGOcc models can be quite difficult to work with, particularly for communities larger than 5-10 species or so, and when some of your species are quite rare. In general, I now recommend using the "spatial factor multispecies occupancy" (sfMsPGOcc) model approach as opposed to spMsPGOcc given that it: (1) is substantially faster; (2) performs equally as well or better than spMsPGOcc in a variety of situations as shown in the paper I link to in the next sentence; (3) and often will be easier to get to converge than spMsPGOcc unless you have ideal circumstances (e.g., only a few species and not super rare).   • 53 sites is a relatively small number of sites to use for a complex spatial occupancy model, so fitting any sort of spatial model will likely be difficult. Because there are not all that many spatial locations, there is limited information that is available to the model to try and estimate the spatial parameters, which is likely why convergence is leading to difficulties. The spMsPGocc function estimates a separate spatial random effect for each species, which is very difficult to do, even when there are a substantially larger number of spatial locations (e.g., hundreds). This is further reason to try out the sfMsPGOcc function, as it will likely be easier to estimate than spMsPGOcc.
  • I see are not including any covariates on detection probability. If there is unmodeled heterogeneity in detection probability, this could also contribute to spatial models being difficult to converge, so that could be something else to think about if you continue to not get the models to work.
  • It may also be helpful to ensure that non-spatial models (e.g., msPGOcc) can converge successfully before going to far down a rabbit hole with convergence issues in the spatial model. Sometimes you may just have too many rare species that you are trying to model.
  • Setting initial values is always useful, particularly for the spatial parameters. Whether you continue with spMsPGOcc or go to sfMsPGOcc, setting initial values based on the values of a preliminary run can often help with convergence difficulties. This vignette talks about some convergence problems with different types of spatial occupancy models.
 Hope that helps!

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: spMsPGOcc - difficulty with convergence
parts:
Hi Tasha,

If you want to produce an effects plot on average across the community, you should first get the mean across species for the occupancy probability of each species at each site, and then you can summarize that to get quantiles and generate the plot. The way you have it now does not give what you want. Instead, you can do something like below to generate psi.0.quants:

# Posterior samples of average occupancy probability across species for each MCMC iteration and each prediction value.
psi.0.mean.samples <- apply(out.pred_mine$psi.0.samples, c(1, 3), mean)
# Then get the quantiles of psi.0.mean.samples
psi.0.quants <- apply(psi.0.mean.samples, 2, quantile, prob = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))

Jeff

# Create a set of values across the range of observed forest edge values

# Scale predicted values by mean and standard deviation used to fit the model
edge.pred.vals.scale <- (edge.pred.vals - mean(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge)) /
  sd(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge)

# Predict occupancy across forest edge values at mean values of all other variable
pred.df_mine <- as.matrix(data.frame(intercept = 1, dist_to_edge = edge.pred.vals.scale,
                                     dist_to_roads = 0, X500_FC_PER = 0))

psi.0.quants <- apply(out.pred_mine$psi.0.samples, c(3), quantile, #here is where I think I may have overlooked something
                      prob = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
psi.plot.dat <- data.frame(psi.med = psi.0.quants[2, ],
                           psi.low = psi.0.quants[1, ],
                           psi.high = psi.0.quants[3, ],
                           dist_to_edge = edge.pred.vals.scale)

#back-transforming for plotting
psi.plot.dat$dte_bt<-(psi.plot.dat$dist_to_edge*sd(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge)) + mean(data.msom$occ.covs$dist_to_edge)
 
edge_mp_graph<-ggplot(psi.plot.dat, aes(x = dte_bt, y = psi.med)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = psi.low, ymax = psi.high), fill = 'grey70') +
  geom_line() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = 'Distance to forest edge (m)', y = 'Occupancy \n Probability')
On Tuesday, January 14, 2025 at 10:16:37 AM UTC jwd...@ncsu.edu wrote:
Hi Tasha,

Glad to hear you were able to get the model to converge. The large uncertainty is likely related to the fairly small number of spatial locations used to fit the spatial model. Spatial occupancy models can be data hungry, particularly when it comes to having a large number of sites, so fitting a model with 53 sites may show substantial uncertainty in the model parameters as a result and will often perform worse with cross-validation (since that requires fitting models with an even smaller number of spatial locations). I think it is reasonable to conclude that you can continue with msPGOcc given the small number of sites and hence difficulty to estimate a spatial process, the cross-validation results, and large uncertainty in the factor loadings.

Kind regards,

Jeff
